concepts.name: Summoning, Prorogation, and Dissolution of Parliament (Articles 85 & 83)
key_dimensions: Distinction between prorogation (ends session) vs. dissolution (ends Lok Sabha) — effects on pending bills
President's power is discretionary vs. binding on Council of Ministers' advice — post-44th Amendment position
Maximum gap between two sessions (6 months) and its constitutional basis
UPSC trap: Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved — only Lok Sabha; implications for joint sitting

concepts.name: Presidential Address to Parliament (Article 87)
key_dimensions: Mandatory occasions: first session after general election AND first session of each year — not every session
Content of address: government's policy statement drafted by Council of Ministers, not President's personal view
Distinction from UK's 'King's Speech' — ceremonial vs. substantive differences
UPSC trap: Article 87 address vs. special address under Article 86 — which is obligatory vs. optional

concepts.name: President's Right to Address and Send Messages to Parliament (Article 86)
key_dimensions: Article 86(1): President may address either House or both Houses assembled together
Article 86(2): President may send messages to either House — House shall consider the matter
Distinction: Article 86 is a discretionary power vs. Article 87 which is obligatory
Comparison with Governor's corresponding powers under Articles 175 and 176

concepts.name: Ordinance-Making Power of the President (Article 123)
key_dimensions: Preconditions: Parliament not in session + President satisfied immediate action necessary — both conditions required
Ordinance has same force as an Act of Parliament but is temporary — must be laid before Parliament
Six-week approval deadline from reassembly; can be withdrawn anytime by President
UPSC trap: Ordinance cannot be issued on subjects requiring Special Majority (Constitutional amendments) — limitations
Re-promulgation of Ordinances — Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa case and Krishna Kumar Singh case rulings

concepts.name: Limitations on Ordinance-Making Power (Article 123 — Exceptions and Boundaries)
key_dimensions: Cannot amend the Constitution via Ordinance — Article 368 requires Parliamentary procedure
Cannot be issued when both Houses are in session simultaneously — only when at least one House is not in session
Judicial review of Ordinances: President's satisfaction is not immune — malafide use is justiciable (Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar 2017)
UPSC trap: Ordinance promulgated during recess of one House — validity when the other House is in session

concepts.name: Presidential Assent to Bills (Article 111)
key_dimensions: Three options: give assent, withhold assent, return bill for reconsideration — but NOT for Money Bills
If Parliament passes bill again with or without amendments, President MUST give assent — pocket veto is debated
UPSC trap: No time limit specified in Constitution for President to act on a bill — 'pocket veto' controversy (Giani Zail Singh episode)
Distinction between ordinary bills, money bills, and constitutional amendment bills regarding assent options

concepts.name: Absolute Veto, Suspensive Veto, and Pocket Veto — Types of Presidential Veto
key_dimensions: Absolute veto: withholding assent to private member bills or government bills after cabinet change — bill lapses
Suspensive veto: returning bill for reconsideration — Parliament can override by re-passing; President must assent
Pocket veto: keeping bill pending indefinitely — possible due to absence of time limit in Article 111
UPSC trap: India has all three types technically, but suspensive veto cannot override constitutional amendment bills — President must assent under Article 368

concepts.name: Presidential Assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills (Article 368)
key_dimensions: President has NO veto over Constitutional Amendment Bills — assent is mandatory after passage
24th Constitutional Amendment Act 1971 made it obligatory for President to give assent
Contrast with ordinary bills under Article 111 where President can withhold or return
UPSC trap: Even if President personally disagrees, Article 368 leaves no discretion — unlike ordinary legislation

concepts.name: Joint Sitting of Parliament (Article 108) — President's Role
key_dimensions: President can summon a joint sitting when a bill is deadlocked between the two Houses
Applicable only to ordinary bills — NOT for Money Bills, Financial Bills (Category 1), or Constitutional Amendment Bills
President summons but does not preside — Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over joint sitting
UPSC trap: President cannot summon joint sitting on their own initiative post-disagreement — specific procedural conditions must be met first

concepts.name: Laying of Reports Before Parliament — President's Legislative Function
key_dimensions: President causes various reports to be laid before Parliament: CAG report (Article 151), Finance Commission report (Article 281), UPSC report (Article 323)
This is a mandatory duty, not discretionary — ensures parliamentary accountability of constitutional bodies
Distinction: President lays report but Parliament debates and scrutinizes — President's role is procedural
UPSC trap: President lays CAG report before Parliament, not before Cabinet — confusion with executive accountability

concepts.name: Prior Recommendation/Permission of President for Introducing Certain Bills (Articles 117, 274)
key_dimensions: Article 117: Bills involving expenditure from Consolidated Fund require President's recommendation before introduction
Article 274: Bills affecting taxation of states require President's recommendation — protects federal financial balance
Distinction: President's recommendation for introduction vs. assent after passage — both are different stages
UPSC trap: Money Bill also requires President's recommendation (Article 117) AND can only be introduced in Lok Sabha — double condition

concepts.name: Special Provisions for Money Bills — President's Role (Articles 109, 110)
key_dimensions: Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject Money Bills — only make recommendations within 14 days
If Rajya Sabha fails to return in 14 days, bill deemed passed by both Houses
President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration — only assent or withhold assent (no suspensive veto)
UPSC trap: Speaker certifies a bill as Money Bill — President cannot question this certification (Article 110(3))

concepts.name: President's Role in Budget and Financial Legislation (Articles 112–116)
key_dimensions: Annual Financial Statement (Budget) laid before Parliament on President's authority — Article 112
No demand for grant can be made without President's recommendation — Article 113(3)
Votes on Account, Votes of Credit, Exceptional Grants — President causes these to be presented
UPSC trap: Budget presented by Finance Minister but on President's behalf — distinction between who presents vs. on whose authority

concepts.name: Nomination Power of President to Parliament (Articles 80, 331)
key_dimensions: Article 80(3): President nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha with expertise in literature, science, art, social service
Article 331: President nominates up to 2 Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha — abolished by 104th Amendment Act 2020
Nominated members' rights: can vote in elections of President? NO — cannot vote in Presidential election
UPSC trap: Nominated RS members can vote in Vice-Presidential election but NOT Presidential election — critical distinction

concepts.name: President's Role When Lok Sabha is Dissolved — Interim Legislative Powers
key_dimensions: After dissolution, Ordinance-making power under Article 123 remains intact — President can still promulgate Ordinances
Caretaker government convention — President acts on advice of outgoing Council of Ministers until new government
Dissolution does not affect Rajya Sabha (permanent House) — continues legislative business within its domain
UPSC trap: Pending bills in Lok Sabha lapse on dissolution; bills in Rajya Sabha or passed by both Houses do not automatically lapse

concepts.name: Lapse of Bills on Dissolution of Lok Sabha — Presidential and Legislative Implications
key_dimensions: Bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse; bills pending in Rajya Sabha (not passed by LS) also lapse
Bills passed by both Houses but awaiting Presidential assent do NOT lapse — President can still act
Bills passed by both Houses at joint sitting are also protected from lapse
UPSC trap: A bill returned by President pending before Lok Sabha at time of dissolution — it lapses, President's action becomes infructuous

concepts.name: President's Discretion vs. Binding Advice in Legislative Powers — Post-42nd and 44th Amendment Position
key_dimensions: 42nd Amendment (1976): Made President bound by Cabinet advice; 44th Amendment (1978): President can return advice ONCE for reconsideration
After reconsideration, President MUST act on revised advice — no second return possible
Legislative powers like summoning, prorogation, dissolution — theoretically discretionary but practically on PM's advice
UPSC trap: Identifying which legislative actions have genuine discretion (e.g., withholding assent to private member bill) vs. conventional discretion

concepts.name: Inter-relationship Between President's Ordinance Power and Parliamentary Legislation — Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Ordinance cannot override fundamental rights — same limitations as Parliament under Part III apply
Ordinance on State List subjects: not permissible under Article 123 — only Union and Concurrent List subjects
If Parliament passes a law inconsistent with an existing Ordinance, the Ordinance becomes void to the extent of inconsistency
UPSC trap: Ordinance-making power exists for President (Art 123) AND Governor (Art 213) — Governor's Ordinance requires President's instructions in some cases (Art 213(1) proviso)

concepts.name: Seeking President's Assent for State Bills Reserved by Governor (Article 201)
key_dimensions: Governor may reserve certain state bills for President's consideration — especially those affecting High Court jurisdiction
President has broader options: assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration, or direct Governor to seek legislative reconsideration
No constitutional time limit for President to decide on reserved state bills — 'pocket veto' more pronounced here
UPSC trap: Unlike Article 111 (central bills), there is NO provision that President MUST assent if state legislature re-passes the reserved bill

concepts.name: President's Role in Anti-Defection Law and Disqualification of Members (Tenth Schedule — Indirect Legislative Role)
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule: Disqualification decided by Speaker/Chairman, not President — but President decides disqualification under Articles 102/103
Article 103: President decides on disqualification of MPs on grounds other than defection — Election Commission's opinion is binding
UPSC trap: Anti-defection disqualification (Tenth Schedule) decided by Presiding Officer; other disqualifications (Article 102) decided by President on EC's opinion
Kihoto Hollohan case (1992): Tenth Schedule is constitutional; Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review
